title: The Stockdale Paradox
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart explains the Stockdale Paradox -- Jim Collins' Good to Great concept named for Vietnam POW Admiral James Stockdale -- in which the prisoners who survived best were neither pure optimists nor pure pessimists, but those who simultaneously confronted the brutal facts of their situation while holding an unwavering faith that they would eventually prevail. He traces the same pattern through Collins' "good to great" companies and through the AA program's first two steps, before applying it directly to teaching: acknowledging daily classroom brutal facts without flinching, while maintaining genuine confidence in the goodness of education for all students. He credits much of his own professional growth to reading outside education, arguing that analogies from unrelated fields often clarify teaching more effectively than teaching books do. The piece closes by previewing a follow-up article applying the paradox to students who don't value school.
points: Stuart explicitly credits non-education books like Good to Great for shaping his teaching more than most teaching books, framing analogical thinking as a deliberate professional-growth strategy.

The core paradox -- surviving POWs were neither pure optimists nor pure pessimists -- gives teachers language for holding two seemingly contradictory stances (realism and hope) without collapsing into either cynicism or denial.

He extends the pattern to AA's first two steps (acknowledging powerlessness, then cultivating faith in a "power greater than themselves"), showing the paradox recurring across unrelated high-stakes contexts.
He explicitly applies the framework to his own writing and teaching practice, positioning "realistic and idealistic" as the operating stance he aims for daily, not just a theoretical concept.
quotes: Interestingly, it wasn't the optimists or the pessimists who proved most resilient. If an optimistic POW was constantly telling himself that he'd be freed any day now, he eventually lost heart and perished. And if a pessimistic POW was constantly convincing himself he'd never be freed, then sure enough — he lost hope, too.
On the one hand, they were relentless in confronting the brutal facts. They were rigorously honest about life as a POW, how dire and terrible and tortuous and bleak it was.
But on the other hand, they held an unwavering faith that, eventually, they'd be freed. They reminded themselves that folks were working to find them, that their release would come eventually.
By holding on to a deep belief that they'd eventually succeed while simultaneously confronting harsh realities, they were able to make the necessary changes and persevere through adversity.

We face the brutal facts daily — we don't shy away from them or pretend they're not there. My blog and books are filled with brutal reality. But one reason I'm proud of my books is that, at the same time, they're filled with an unwavering confidence in the goodness of an education, for all students.
And so then, what do we do? We operate from both realities. We engage with both. And in doing that, we become these otherworldly kinds of creatures: teachers who are both realistic and idealistic.
